newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Breuer says Bavaria merger set key precedent.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Breuer says Bavaria merger set key precedent.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG on Wednesday praised this week's Bavarian banking mega-merger as a "stroke of genius" that might point the way for German banks to cut back their massive and unpopular industrial shareholdings.

Bayerische Vereinsbank AG on Monday announced plans to merge with Bayerischer Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG in a way that neatly sidesteps hefty tax charges it would normally be incurred in such a deal.

Deutsche Bank chairman Rolf Breuer said he hoped the deal might pave the way for a general loosening of fiscal demands regarding corporate shareholdings, now subject to a 60 percent capital gains tax if sold directly.
"This is a new phase for swapping arrangements, which is of absolutely top interest to us," Breuer told a news conference.
"It is the first time that this has been attempted. I hope it works."

Breuer, one of Germany's best-known supporters of capital market reforms, has consistently cited taxes as the prime obstacle stopping banks from selling high-value industrial stakes such as Deutsche's 22.6 percent holding in Daimler-Benz.
German banks have long been under pressure from international lobbyists for shareholder value to pare back the vast network of cross-shareholdings and huge industrial investments they control.
Moreover, a merger on the Bavarian model could provide an elegant way for banks and insurers to join forces, as many analysts believe they must to survive in an enlarged market.

While Deutsche was not interested in a German acquisition, it would have no fundamental objections to swapping industrial shareholdings for stakes in banks if it was possible to do so in a tax-efficient way, Breuer said.
In the first stage of the Bavarian merger, Vereinsbank is to buy up to 45 percent of Hypo-Bank by offering Hypo shareholders shares in insurer Allianz AG from its own investment portfolio.
The terms of the deal allow Vereinsbank to liquidate about nine billion marks of hidden assets -- or 4/5ths of its 10 percent Allianz stake -- without attracting tax.

Vereinsbank is taking advantage of a German legal opinion on stake swaps called a "Tauschgutachten", which allows companies to avoid tax by swapping assets, albeit only where the assets to be swapped are of equal type and value.

Despite Vereinsbank's coup, which Breuer said warranted respect, the Deutsche chairman said past experience showed that swap operations were generally subject to tight restrictions from fiscal authorities.
The Bavarian merger did not quite fulfil the demands of the "Tauschgutachten" since it involved banking and insurance assets, rather than identical share types, Breuer observed.
Asked if a sea-change was likely in the German corporate tax system, Breuer said flatly. "The chances are very remote."
Regional authorities can decide whether or not a transaction can come under the "Tauschgutachten" banner.

It is generally accepted that Bavaria took a looser view of the legal position in order to ensure that the merger could go ahead. The creation of a massive Bavarian bank is viewed locally as a massive boon for Munich's ambitions to hold its own against Frankfurt as a financial centre.
Breuer took a veiled swipe at the differences which prevail between German regions in terms of the legal set-up for companies.

"It is not the task of this bank to question this country's constitutional system," he said. "We live with it, we accept it. But one could question whether or not this (system) can survive for the next 50 years."

Vereinsbank chief executive Albrecht Schmidt, presenting the merger plans to a news conference on Monday, described the deal as "one of the most creative capital market transactions seen in recent years."

Breuer said Deutsche saw no reason whay it should make any immediate changes to its 5.2 percent stake in Vereinsbank. Deutsche's announcement of that stake last year triggered a massive flurry of takeover speculation and undoubtedly accelerated the Bavarian merger deal.
But he said the holding had ceased to be strategic, and was now merely financial.
